sections.heading: Investigate the request before choosing what to build
sections.content: Ask the people requesting the feature how they actually work and what they are trying to accomplish. Yu says that when a broad feature request turns out to encompass many different use cases, the choice is between covering the long tail with one large feature and identifying concentrated groups of use cases that make sense to solve especially well. He also emphasizes grounding decisions in real users and workflows, rather than hypothetical personas or a general count of requests.

sections.heading: Example: customer tracking instead of more custom fields
sections.content: Linear repeatedly heard requests for fully customizable fields. This let teams track and report on requests while helping builders see the real use cases without making ICs do extra work.

answer.summary: When a broad feature is requested, Yu recommends digging into real requesters’ workflows and finding whether specific, concentrated use cases deserve a focused solution rather than building for every possible case. Linear’s Customer Requests feature illustrates this approach: it addressed a customer-tracking need behind some requests for custom fields without adding manual work for individual contributors.

sections.heading: Investigate the real need behind the request
sections.content: Talk to the person asking and ask how they are trying to use the feature. Yu favors grounding decisions in identifiable people and real workflows—not hypothetical users or a general count of requests—and checking whether the product assumptions match reality.

sections.heading: Narrow a broad request to the use cases worth solving
sections.content: When a big feature request turns out to span many different use cases, Yu describes two options: build something covering the long tail, or identify concentrated groups of use cases that make sense to support as a first-order feature and solve those particularly well. The practical question is whether the request reveals a specific problem to address, rather than assuming one broad solution fits everyone.

sections.heading: Example: custom fields led to Customer Requests
sections.content: Linear kept hearing requests for fully customized fields. When the team asked why, 40% of the requests they examined were about tracking customer needs—for example, knowing that Walmart had requested a feature and reporting what had been done for that customer. Rather than add many fields that could burden individual contributors, Linear built Customer Requests: it could bring in feedback from support tools and CRMs, analyze email origins, and tag escalated feature requests to the relevant customer automatically. That let teams track and report requests while helping builders see the real customer context without manual tagging.
